fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. David defeated the Philistines, subdued them, and took Metheg-ammah from their hand (2 Samuel 8:1). It's the first win on a list that gets long in a hurry.

Not the Midianites, friend. Verse 1 says David defeated the Philistines and took Metheg-ammah from their hand. The Midianites never show up anywhere in this passage. A list this fast will make anybody grab for a familiar name.
Chariots come up in verse 4, friend, and those are chariots David captures from Hadadezer, king of Zobah. The Moabites in verse 2 bring tribute. Same passage, different crowd.

The Jordan isn't the river in this verse, friend. The text says Hadadezer marched out to restore his dominion along the Euphrates River (2 Samuel 8:3). That was his plan, and David defeated him anyway.

The Nile doesn't come up here, baker. Verse 3 says Hadadezer had marched out to restore his dominion along the Euphrates River. His plan was set on that river, and the verse opens with David defeating him.

That's them. The Arameans of Damascus came to help King Hadadezer of Zobah, and David struck down twenty-two thousand of their men (2 Samuel 8:5). That's a heavy number. Then in verse 6 the Arameans became subject to David.
Jerusalem is right. David took the gold shields that belonged to Hadadezer's officers and brought them to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 8:7). Those shields changed owners and ended up in Jerusalem.

Hebron never comes up in this passage, friend. Verse 7 says David took the gold shields that belonged to Hadadezer's officers and brought them to Jerusalem. The shields went from the officers to David, and the verse sends them to Jerusalem, not Hebron.

Gibeon isn't in this passage, baker. The text says David brought the gold shields of Hadadezer's officers to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 8:7). If you're hunting for where those shields end up, stop at Jerusalem.

True. King David dedicated these to the LORD, along with the silver and gold he had dedicated from all the nations he had subdued (2 Samuel 8:11). "These" means the silver, gold and bronze that Joram brought from King Toi. Verse 12 then lists where the other silver and gold came from.

A name, baker. “And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt.” (2 Samuel 8:13). The verse says exactly that. It ties the name to his return.

A treaty isn't mentioned here, baker. Verse 13 says David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. Nobody signs anything in that verse, and the thing he makes is a name.
